teach.title: Who did it, when the verb is passive
teach.say: A passive verb says the action is done *to* its subject: *saccus portātur* — the sack is carried. To name the person doing it, Latin puts *ā* in front (or *ab* when the next word starts with a vowel: *ab amīcō*) and the doer goes into **the ablative (the 'by' form after ā/ab)**, *ablātīvus auctōris*: *ā servō* — by the slave. Nothing else in the sentence moves.

teach.title: A servus-type doer ends in -ō
teach.say: The doer is an ordinary noun, so it takes the ablative ending of its own family. A noun in -us (*servus*, *dominus*, *amīcus*) drops -us and ends **-ō** in the ablative singular: *ā servō*, *ā dominō*, *ab amīcō*. Names in -us do the same: *ā Iūliō*.

teach.title: An ancilla-type doer ends in -ā
teach.say: A noun in -a (*ancilla*, *domina*, and the names *Syra*, *Aemilia*) ends **-ā** in the ablative singular: *ab ancillā*, *ā dominā*, *ā Syrā*. It is the same letter as the plain nominative, only long — so look for *ā/ab* in front, which never lies.

teach.title: More than one doer: -īs
teach.say: When several people do it, the doer goes into the ablative plural, and both families end **-īs**: *ā servīs*, *ā puerīs*, *ā puellīs*. Watch the verb: it is plural only when the *subject* is plural (*saccī portantur*), never because the doers are many — *ā servīs suīs dominus nōn timētur* has one master and many slaves, and the verb stays singular.

teach.title: A doer, or a thing used?
teach.say: *ā/ab* names something alive that chose to act — a person, a god, an animal. A lifeless thing the doer uses takes the bare ablative with no preposition at all: *baculō* — with a stick. In *servus baculō ā dominō verberātur* both are present: the master does it, the stick is what he does it with. Ask of each ablative: could this decide to act?

teach.title: It can stand anywhere in the sentence
teach.say: The doer is marked by *ā/ab* and by the ending, never by its place, so the phrase may open the sentence, sit in the middle, or follow the verb without the meaning shifting: *ā servīs suīs dominus nōn timētur* = the master is not feared by his own slaves. Read the endings first and the order second.

core.text: When a verb is passive, the person who actually does the action is named with *ā/ab* and **the ablative (the 'by' form after a/ab)**, *ablātīvus auctōris*: *dominus ā servō timētur* = the master is feared by the slave. *Ā* stands before a consonant, *ab* before a vowel (*ab Ursō*) and often elsewhere too. The doer need not be mentioned at all: *dominus timētur* = the master is feared.
In *the goat is led by the boy*, *by the boy* names the doer, the agent. English *by* also does other jobs (*by a stone*, *by the river*), which Latin keeps apart.
Passive verb + *ā/ab* + ablative of a living being = the agent, the 'by whom'. A lifeless thing used takes the plain ablative instead.

invented.en: The sheep is saved by the dog.

core.text: *Goliath ā Dāvide lapide percutitur* — struck by David (agent: *ā* + ablative) with a stone (means: bare ablative). The rule is about life: people, gods and animals doing something take *ā/ab*; tools, weapons and body parts do not. *Ab* + a thing means 'from', not 'by'.

more.text: From the learner's notes: with an active verb the agent is simply the subject; with a passive verb it may be dropped or added with *ab*. Latin treats the agent as a kind of origin — the leading 'comes from' the boy — which is why the 'from' preposition is used, though it can never be translated 'from'. The notes' pair: *Goliath ā Dāvide lapide percutitur*; *servus ā dominō oculīs vidētur* — seen by his master (agent) with his eyes (means).

Ørberg cap. VI and VIII: *ā quō?* — *ab eō / ab illō servō*; *saccus ā servō portātur*. With no passive verb, *ā/ab* is plain origin: *ā vīllā venit*. Later, the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk) names its doer with the dative instead (dative of agent). A&G §405.
